newsitem.title: UK: Iraq crude export target date viewed sceptically.
newsitem.headline: Iraq crude export target date viewed sceptically.

text.p: Oil traders gearing up to handle a flood of Iraqi crude exports were sceptical on Wednesday the shipments would begin in the seven to 10 day time-frame indicated by Baghdad.

Dealers hoping to renew contracts with Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organisation were wrestling with the political and logistic imponderables still to be solved and the effect on oil prices once crude does start to flow.

"Two to three weeks from now is the earliest we believe the oil will start to arrive," said one senior figure at a London trading house hoping to again pick up oil at the Turkish port of Ceyhan and the Gulf Mina al-Bakr terminal.

Iraqi oil minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed on Tuesday predicted quick agreement with the United Nations on the fine print of an aid distribution plan that would allow crude flows to resume within 10 days.
A senior U.N. official said on Monday the details of the accord on humanitarian hand-outs could be settled within days with Iraqi cooperation.

But while Rasheed's statement reassured observers sufficient goodwill existed to finalise the U.N. aid deal, they felt disputes over unspent proceeds from the first oil-for-food accord could lead Baghdad to miss its target date.
Baghdad had been stalling the resumption of crude shipments until contracts to spend $800 million of proceeds from the first six month export schedule were cleared by U.N. bureaucrats.
"From my discussions with the Iraqis I believe they will still push for some of the $800 million of contracts to be lined up," said another dealer in touch with Baghdad.
And a dispute between Iraq and the U.N. over arms inspections may still cast a shadow over the crude programme, although the arms and aid issues are not linked.

Most traders predicted it would be mid-July before Iraq will start pumping, with contract negotiations, an early-July shipping shortage in the Mediterranean and logistical hurdles still to be overcome.

"I think people will have to go to Baghdad to re-sign contracts as there still seems to be debate on price," said the dealer, who said most companies hoped to resume lifting at the values extant when crude flows stopped in May.
Iraq's official selling price in May for Kirkuk Blend, exported via Ceyhan, was Dated Brent -$2.20 a barrel, which Baghdad was seen likely to try to increase.
Market players also wondered if Iraq might seek to defer the start of the 180-day period to avoid a "bulge" in exports volumes that could depress outright values.
OPEC, currently meeting in Vienna, could be expected to support such a request in order to shore up oil prices.
Iraq has said it will begin by pumping 730-750,000 barrels per day, up from the average of 660,000 bpd in the first six-month export period.
If it cannot delay the start of the accord it may have to up the volume to around one million bpd to meet its cash target of $1 billion earned in each of two 90-day periods.

That would dramatically depress oil prices, which in a circular effect would force them to pump yet more oil. However, pipeline, storage and shipping capacity limits may prevent them reaching their goal.

"According to U.N. regulations I think that if Iraq doesn't ship $1 billion worth then that oil is foregone and it could just be unfeasible to deliver that amount in the first phase," said one trader.
"And paradoxically that could be price supportive," he added. "Right now there are more questions than answers, it is all very uncertain." - Sean Maguire, William Maclean +44 171 542 8060
